tagline: Cambodia's island-hopping coast — luxury resorts blooming across Koh Rong, Koh Russey and the Ream private-island cluster, all reached today by aging diesel speedboats over short, calm hops.
summary: Cambodia's southern coast around Sihanoukville is the country's island-hopping engine: the mainland gateway port and airport feed a ring of resort islands — Koh Rong and Koh Rong Sanloem (Saracen Bay), the private islands of Song Saa and Koh Russey (Bamboo Island), Koh Ta Kiev, and the Ream National Park / Lila private-island cluster. Every transfer is a short, protected hop (Sihanoukville to the islands runs ~10-40 minutes by boat; all legs sit comfortably under 30 nm), making this a textbook Pioneer II all-electric market. Demand is overwhelmingly luxury-tourism led and accelerating: Koh Rong nearly doubled to ~184,600 visitors in 2024 and welcomed over 100,000 in the first quarter of 2025 alone, against a luxury hotel pipeline that includes InterContinental Sihanoukville and Six Senses Krabey Island. Today's transfers run on diesel speedboats with inconsistent comfort and wake; a foiling-electric layer offers fast, stable, quiet, zero-wake transit ideal for protected reef waters and the high-end guest experience these resorts are built around. Navier's May 2026 partnership with the WorldBridge Group — one of Cambodia's largest conglomerates and developer of Lila Resort on a pristine private island — anchors the market with first-vessel delivery in 2026 and a multi-vessel, local-sales collaboration to follow.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: All hops sit well under Pioneer II's 70 nm all-electric range over calm, protected reef water — Sihanoukville ↔ Lila/Ream (~8 nm), ↔ Koh Rong (~14 nm) and inter-island Koh Rong ↔ Song Saa/Koh Russey (~10 nm) — the cleanest possible product-market fit, where a quiet, zero-wake arrival is a tangible upgrade over diesel speedboats and the signed WorldBridge/Lila partnership provides an on-the-ground anchor.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta LR's ~2,000 nm hybrid range, with no charging-infrastructure dependency, extends reach up the coast to Kep and Koh Kong, across to Phu Quoc (Vietnam) and for longer repositioning where island grid charging isn't viable.

competitive_landscape: Transfers today run on conventional diesel speedboats and shared resort boats; no electric or foiling layer exists. Grab operates in Cambodia for land mobility, making a multimodal land+water tie-in natural.
seasonality: Nov-Apr dry season is peak; May-Oct southwest monsoon brings rougher seas on exposed legs (protected bays and short hops remain workable).
regulatory_note: Coastal transport under Cambodian maritime authority oversight; resort-operated transfers are well established. Confirm cabotage/charter licensing route with WorldBridge local entity.
